roadmap.goal: Ship slice 04b of ADO Epic #5775 (Story #5789): an instance can never write a secret with the key that ships inside every copy of Lighthouse, and can never be told it is safe when it is not. Every check in the codebase reasoned about key identity or envelope shape; nothing compared key material, so the published key supplied through configuration and wearing a k-cfg- id derived from its own bytes walked past the one check built to catch it (F-20), while an install that had set a key of its own before this release was told its credentials were public when they never were (F-21). Supplied key material equal to the published key is refused as an ACTIVE key at the one moment it can still be said — before a credential is written under it — naming the setting that carried it. The same material stays welcome as a RETIRED entry, or every upgrade stops being readable. And the published-key count stops deciding by envelope prefix and starts asking the only honest question: can that key read this value?
roadmap.overview: Three phases, 4 steps, inside-out: the one class that owns the published key learns the two questions everything else needs to ask, then the parser every transport funnels through refuses it as an active key, then the count defers to it instead of guessing from envelope shape. The last step is documentation and the slice close.

slice_to_phase._not_in_this_roadmap_: the panel's wording and which actions it offers (slice 06a, incl. F-21's second-order wording and F-27); recovering an instance that already cannot read its secrets (slice 05b); the Helm chart custody surface (slice 05, Story #5780). Encryption:AllowLegacyDefault stays undone and is recorded as a recommendation to delete in the DISTILL Upstream Issues.

phases.name: The two questions about the published key
phases.description: LegacyDefaultEncryptionKey is already the single place the published material is compiled in, and it hands out no accessor for it. It learns the two questions its callers need answered, both of which hand back a boolean, so the material still never leaves the class.

steps.name: Is this the published key, and can it read this value
steps.description: RED: create `LegacyDefaultEncryptionKeyTests.cs`. Cases for `Matches`: the published material matches; 32 other bytes do not; material of the wrong length does not (and does not throw). Cases for `CanRead`: a value in the format this version replaced written under the published key is readable; the same written under another key is not; an envelope naming the published key is readable; an envelope naming another key holding published material is readable, because the question is the key and not the name; an envelope on another key entirely is not; a value that was never encrypted is not; null and empty are not. GREEN: add `Matches(ReadOnlySpan<byte>)` over `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`, and `CanRead(string?)` which, for an envelope, tries to unprotect it with the published material under the envelope's own key id, and otherwise classifies it against a ring holding nothing but the published key and accepts only the legacy-CBC state. COMMIT: `feat(encryption): let the published key answer whether it is the key, and what it can read`.
red_to_green_tests: The published material is recognised
Other material of the right length is not
Material of the wrong length is rejected without throwing
A legacy value written under the published key can be read
A legacy value written under another key cannot
An envelope naming the published key can be read
An envelope holding published material under another name can be read
An envelope on another key cannot
A value that was never encrypted cannot
Null and empty cannot
criteria: No key material leaves the class: both members return a boolean.
The comparison is constant-time, so nobody is tempted to compare base64 strings and then trim them.

phases.name: Refused as the key in force
phases.description: Every transport that can hand Lighthouse a key funnels through one parser, and that parser is handed the name of the thing that supplied it. That is where the refusal goes, so a fifth transport added later inherits it and the message can quote the setting without anything being threaded through.

steps.name: The published key cannot be the key secrets are written under
steps.description: RED: extend `EncryptionKeyRingBootstrapperTests.cs`. Cases: the published key under `Encryption:Key` refuses the start, and the refusal names that setting, says the key is the one published with the product, says why that is no protection, says nothing stored has been changed, and names one thing to do instead; the same under the retired name names the retired name; a two-key ring whose FIRST entry is the published key refuses and names the ring setting; a mounted key file holding it refuses and names the file; a two-key ring whose SECOND entry is the published key starts, writes under the operator's key and still reads what was under the published one; an instance with a durable store and pre-upgrade credentials still starts and still reads all of them; an instance that cannot keep a key of its own and already holds credentials still starts on the published key, because that path never parses a supplied string; no refusal contains any part of the key material. GREEN: in `SuppliedKeyRing.ParsedFrom`, after the parse succeeds, refuse when `LegacyDefaultEncryptionKey.Matches(parsed.ActiveKey.Material.Span)`, with the message assembled by a `PublishedKeyAsTheActiveKey` sentence-holder beside `NoDurableKeyStore`. COMMIT: `feat(encryption): refuse to write secrets with the key published with the product`.
red_to_green_tests: The published key under the documented setting refuses the start
The refusal names the setting, the problem, what is not lost, and what to do
The published key under the name this release retired refuses, naming that name
A ring whose first entry is the published key refuses, naming the ring setting
A mounted key file holding the published key refuses, naming the file
A ring whose second entry is the published key starts and keeps both keys
An instance that upgrades still reads every credential it stored
An instance with nowhere to keep a key of its own still starts on the published key
No refusal contains any part of the key material
criteria: The refusal is about the first entry of the ring only; the end of the ring is untouched.
PublishedDefaultOnly() is not caught, because it never parses a supplied string.
Every transport is refused by one message, in one place.

phases.name: A count that is true in both directions
phases.description: The count guessed which key wrote a value from the shape of the value. The narrowing predicate stays in SQL — it is what keeps the settings page free for an instance that has already moved everything — and the guess it used to make on the narrowed set is replaced by asking the key itself.

steps.name: Count what that key can read, not what the value looks like
steps.description: RED: extend `PublishedKeySecretCountTests.cs` against the real SQLite context already in that file. New cases: a legacy value written under a key of the instance's own is NOT counted (F-21); a legacy value written under the published key still IS counted; an envelope naming the published key is counted; an envelope naming the instance's own key is not; a value that was never encrypted is not counted; a mixture across options and both token columns counts exactly the ones the published key can read. Extend `EncryptionControllerTests.cs` with the two ends of that on the wire. GREEN: in `PublishedKeySecretCount`, keep the SQL predicate as the narrowing filter but select the values instead of counting rows, then count the ones `LegacyDefaultEncryptionKey.CanRead` accepts. COMMIT: `fix(encryption): count the secrets that key can actually read`.
red_to_green_tests: A legacy value on a key of the instance's own is not counted
A legacy value on the published key is still counted
An envelope naming the published key is counted
An envelope naming another key is not counted
A value that was never encrypted is not counted
Options and both token columns are counted together, and only what that key can read
The route reports zero for a custom-key install and non-zero for a default one
criteria: An instance with nothing left on that key decrypts nothing to be told so.
The count and the check pass can no longer contradict each other about the same credential.

phases.name: Documentation and slice close
phases.description: What an operator sees if they carry the pre-epic key value across the upgrade, and where the slice's verdict is recorded.

steps.name: Say what happens to the operator who kept their own configuration
steps.description: Update `docs/Installation/configuration.md`: the encryption key section gains what Lighthouse does if the value supplied is the one published with the product, why, and the two ways out. Record the slice verdict in `slices/slice-04b-published-key-never-active.md` and mark F-20 and F-21 addressed in `verification/manual-walkthrough.md`. COMMIT: `docs(encryption): say what happens if the published key is supplied as the key`.
criteria: The documentation says the setting name an operator will actually see quoted in the refusal.
No internal reference numbers appear in prose a user reads.
